candidateRows: A theory of fundamental reality should reduce arbitrariness, and a purported foundation's unexplained limited attributes provide reason to deny its fundamentality.
This establishes the argument's governing strategy and explains why intrinsic arbitrary limits count against a proposed fundamental reality.
After introductory framing, Josh presents the limits argument as a theory-selection tool and illustrates its application to a visibly bounded candidate foundation.
An arbitrary limit is an unexplained nonmaximal parameter situated among conceivable greater or lesser degrees that reason does not preclude.
The definition fixes the central concept used to infer that particular bounded features of a foundation require explanation rather than being fundamental.
Joe's request to clarify whether arbitrariness means unexplained, inexplicable, or capable of being otherwise.
Joe distinguishes several possible notions of arbitrariness, after which Josh specifies the explanatory and scalar senses required by his argument.
If a fundamental reality has some degree of greatness and limits have explanations, its greatness is not arbitrarily limited and the foundation is perfect in a relevant sense.
This is the explicit argument connecting an assumed fundamental reality through explained limits and greatness to a perfect foundation.
Following clarification of arbitrariness, Josh lays out the value-based version premise by premise and identifies perfection as its concluding characterization.
Even if the existence of a fundamental reality is only assumed, the resulting conditional can reveal implications that confirm or undermine that assumption.
This protects the argument's dialectical usefulness when its stage-one assumption is disputed and permits downstream premises to test that assumption.
The possibility that rejecting the assumed fundamental reality would deprive the remaining limits argument of value.
During discussion of the assumed stage-one foundation, Josh explains that conditional reasoning can still expose consequences and generate reasons concerning the assumption.
The premise that limits are explained makes no independent headway toward theism because non-theistic theories entail fundamental limits and must be compared holistically with rivals.
The objection challenges whether the argument itself establishes theism rather than merely identifying one theoretical cost to be weighed against all competing virtues.
Josh's premise that limits have explanations and his proposed inference from removing fundamental limits toward a perfect foundation.
After premise two is restated nonmodally, Joe argues that antecedently accepted non-theistic theories reject it and require overall comparative assessment instead.
The argument from arbitrary limits can expose a theoretical cost without by itself forcing every rational evaluator to reject the affected worldview.
It directly qualifies what the limits argument establishes while defending its usefulness in comparative theory assessment despite worldview-dependent judgments.
Schmid's contention that theory comparison concedes the limits argument itself does not establish theism.
Rasmussen illustrates the point with a hypothetical blue foundation: an unexplained limit counts against the theory, yet independent explanatory benefits may outweigh that cost.
Apparently irrelevant differences between possible fundamental limits provide strong reason to seek a further explanation of any particular limit.
This supplies the main positive motivation for the argument's limits-explanation principle rather than merely presupposing that principle.
Schmid's concern that non-theistic theories may simply reject the premise that fundamental limits require explanation.
Rasmussen compares alternative shapes and colors at reality's base, arguing that no relevant difference selects one and that explanatory experience reinforces the demand for explanation.
A theory's independent simplicity and explanatory success may itself justify expecting a fundamental limit to differ relevantly from other limits.
It challenges Rasmussen's relevant-difference rationale by locating defeasible justification in the total comparative virtues of a rival theory.
Rasmussen's claim that no relevant difference can explain why one particular fundamental limit obtains instead of another.
Schmid grants that unexplained limits can be a theoretical cost but argues that a successful naturalistic theory may warrant confidence that a relevant difference exists even before it is specified.
Independent support for a theory with a fundamental limit is a reasonable response, but it must be weighed against the apparent explanatory demand generated by particular limits.
The response concedes the force of holistic theory comparison while preserving the central intuition that particular arbitrary limits require deeper explanation.
Schmid's proposal that independent theoretical virtues can warrant belief in an unspecified relevant difference for a fundamental limit.

Rasmussen treats the dispute as comparative worldview construction, acknowledges that other considerations may dominate, but maintains that colors, shapes, power, and value strongly appear to demand explanation.
An experiential track record of explanation supports only a defeasible generalization because independent evidence can rationally justify exceptions to that record.
This attacks a principal justification for extending observed explanatory patterns to fundamental reality and clarifies why dialectical opponents may reject that extension.
Rasmussen's appeal to the experienced track record of further explanations as support for explaining fundamental limits.

Using disagreement about black swans, Schmid argues that parties with different background evidence need not accept the same default generalization and urges intellectual engagement with rival perspectives.
A defeasible principle favoring explanations of limits can retain evidential value even if independent reasons sometimes license stopping the explanatory search.
It preserves a qualified version of the limits principle under Schmid's default-principle objection while conceding that it is not a decisive argument-ending consideration.
Schmid's black-swan objection that explanatory track records yield defeasible defaults with rationally permitted exceptions.

Rasmussen accepts reservations about uniformity, treats differing rational perspectives as informative, and says the defeasible principle may still aid inquiry without functioning as a final decisive premise.
The same inductive, abductive, intuitive, and relevant-difference support used for the limits principle can motivate rival causal principles that conflict with traditional theism.
The symmetry objection challenges the inference toward theism by arguing that its own justificatory methods equally support principles yielding anti-theistic consequences.
Rasmussen's use of explanatory uniformity, intuition, and relevant differences to move from arbitrary limits toward a theistic foundation.
Schmid proposes a materially causal principle supported like the limits principle; applied universally, it implies prior material causes and pressures creation ex nihilo or even theism more broadly.
If equally supported principles lead to competing conclusions, the original argument needs a symmetry breaker established by comparing the principles and their support.
This concedes a major undercutting challenge and identifies the additional burden the limits argument must meet before its theistic conclusion is supported.
Schmid's parody argument that similarly motivated causal principles can yield conclusions incompatible with traditional theism.
Rasmussen agrees that symmetric support undercuts the original inference absent a breaker, treats comparison as an open project, and allows rival principles to revise theological models.
The premise that fundamental reality has some greatness is doubtful because a mindless and impersonal foundation may be axiologically neutral.
The objection targets the premise required to convert the absence of arbitrary limits into unlimited greatness, thereby blocking the argument's movement toward divine perfection.
The limits argument's fourth premise that the fundamental reality possesses at least some degree of greatness.
Schmid argues that quantum fields, particles, wave functions, and singularities do not intuitively possess value; greatness may require mindedness, which has not yet been established.
The greatness premise can be supported by arguments for fundamental mentality and by the value involved in possessing the original power to produce value.
The response supplies the missing bridge from fundamental reality to value or greatness, a necessary step for the limits argument to approach God-like perfection.
Schmid's objection that an impersonal fundamental reality could be axiologically neutral and therefore lack any greatness.
Rasmussen cites several arguments for fundamental mentality, concedes a gap if none succeeds, and adds that the source of all value-producing powers may itself occupy an axiological dimension.
The limits argument alone cannot establish theism because it requires an independently supported premise that the necessary foundation is minded.
This identifies a major inferential gap between the argument's foundation and a theistic conclusion, directly limiting what the argument can establish.
Josh's proposal to supplement the limits argument with several arguments that the fundamental foundation is minded.
After Josh offers several routes to fundamental mentality and value, Joe stresses that those routes are additional premises rather than consequences of the limits argument itself.
The proposed greatness principle lacks intuitive support and appears vulnerable to counterexamples and conceivable cases where greatness is grounded in non-greatness.
The principle is offered to secure some value or greatness at reality's foundation, so these three objections challenge a central bridge in the pro case.
Josh's claim that producing, explaining, or grounding value requires something that is itself valuable or greatness-involving.
Joe first denies sharing the intuition, then uses sponginess and knowledge as possible counterexamples, and finally describes a conceivable non-greatness-involving ground of limited greatness.

If a value-entailing property is grounded in something, its ground is also value-entailing, because a wholly valueless reality could not acquire positive aspects without already possessing a valuable potential.
This refined grounding principle supplies the pro side's route from derivative value to value at the foundation and potentially onward to fundamental mindedness.
Joe's objections that greatness can arise from non-greatness and that knowledge may be grounded in components lacking greatness.
Josh sharpens the rough slogan into a grounding principle, argues that the potential to develop positive aspects is itself positive, and sketches a value-first route to a fundamental mind.
Even under Josh's clarified grounding formulation, the greatness principle remains unintuitive and unsupported from Joe's perspective.
This reply blocks the suggestion that the disagreement resulted merely from imprecise wording and preserves the objection against the refined principle itself.
Josh's refined claim that anything grounding a greatness-entailing or value-entailing property must itself be value-entailing.
Joe says his earlier criticism already targeted a synonymous principle, acknowledges that others can possess the intuition, but concludes that he still does not see its force.
A remote capacity to produce valuable states does not seem valuable merely because an initial natural state can eventually lead through many stages to value.
The example directly tests the pro side's proposed fallback from the grounding principle to the claim that value-producing capacity is itself valuable.
Josh's suggestion that merely having the capacity to produce valuable states may confer value on the foundation.
Joe describes an initial singularity whose successive states eventually yield valuable beings and questions why that highly indirect productive capacity should itself count as good.
A foundation's capacity to permit later value is itself part of what makes the foundation valuable, since without that capacity no value would exist.
This is the pro side's direct defense of the capacity-based route for attributing some value to fundamental reality despite Joe's remote-causation example.
Joe's claim that an initial singularity's remote capacity to yield valuable states does not appear valuable in itself.
Josh answers that the absence of the foundational capacity would eliminate all later value and treats enabling value in the world as a value-conferring feature.
Being a necessary condition for value is insufficient for being valuable, since necessary mathematical truths enable all value without thereby seeming valuable themselves.
The counterexample attacks the precise inference from being indispensable for value to possessing value, undermining the capacity-based support for foundational greatness.
Josh's claim that the foundation is valuable because without its value-producing capacity there would be no value.
Joe compares the foundation's necessity for value with necessary mathematical truths, arguing that indispensable conditions of value need not themselves possess value.
A foundation may have non-maximal greatness without arbitrary limitation when its limit is explained by metaphysical necessity or by the foundation's essential nature.
This directly challenges the inference from absence of arbitrary limits to perfection by offering explained yet non-maximal limits at the fundamental level.
Premise six of Josh's argument, which infers that a foundation whose greatness is not arbitrarily limited is perfect in some sense.
After restating premise six, Joe proposes that a submaximal degree of greatness could be non-arbitrary because it is metaphysically necessary or constitutive of what the foundation is.
The dialectical Trinity objection pressures trinitarian users of the limits argument because their worldview assigns God a fixed limit of three persons while opposing arbitrary limits.
The objection exposes a potential internal tension between the limits argument and a major theistic conception that its intended proponents may independently accept.
Josh explains that the dialectical version does not directly attack a premise but asks trinitarians whether they can consistently retain both the limits reasoning and a tri-personal foundation.

Only limits lacking deeper explanation count as arbitrary, while the structural Trinity objection shows that any deeper explanation allowed for divine limits may also be available for natural foundations.
This clarification defines the argument's key notion of arbitrariness and confronts a symmetry that could prevent the reasoning from favoring a divine over a natural foundation.
The Trinity-based challenges that fixed divine limits conflict with the rejection of arbitrary limits and that naturalists can invoke parallel deeper explanations.

Josh distinguishes unexplained from deeply explained limits, presents the symmetry between theistic and natural foundations, and reframes the argument as a worldview-relative tool for reducing arbitrariness as far as possible.
The argument from arbitrary limits can remain useful as a worldview-relative tool for reducing unexplained arbitrariness even when some foundational brute fact is independently accepted.
This reframes the argument's ambition and explains how it can support maximal greatness without requiring every user to reject all foundational brute facts.
The structural Trinity objection that a natural foundation could explain its limits just as a theist explains divine limits.
After stating the structural objection, Rasmussen explains that the method can probe a person's own worldview by removing arbitrariness wherever no independent commitment requires a limit.
A deeper property of fundamental reality could explain a limit on its greatness and thereby leave that reality imperfect, paralleling explanations of a limited number of divine persons.
The possibility directly challenges the inference from an explained limit to perfect foundational reality and motivates Rasmussen's subsequent defenses.
The limits argument's inference that fundamental reality cannot possess a bounded or nonmaximal degree of greatness.
Rasmussen strengthens the structural objection by proposing that a more basic nature or property could both explain a limitation and preclude divine perfection.

Rasmussen's original greatness-principle response distinguishes greatness from tripersonality because producing positive qualities plausibly presupposes some positive value in their ground, whereas producing three persons need not presuppose tripersonality.
This is a direct defense of the move to a perfect foundation against the structural Trinity objection and identifies the key asymmetry on which that defense depends.
The objection that explanations of divine tripersonality equally permit an imperfect foundation whose limited greatness has a deeper ground.
Rasmussen argues that a foundation grounding positive derivative qualities must possess fundamental greatness, while a ground of tripersonality need not itself be tripersonal.

When an arbitrary property is strongly grounded by a property that uniquely necessitates it, the grounding property inherits the arbitrariness, preventing arbitrary limits from being hidden in the base of reality.
The inheritance principle supplies Rasmussen's newer route from the removal of arbitrariness to a perfect or quasi-perfect foundation without relying on the disputed greatness principle.
The proposal that a more basic feature or trope could explain a foundational reality's limited greatness without leaving any unexplained limit.

Using color and Platonist examples, Rasmussen argues that a selective necessitating ground inherits the arbitrariness of what it grounds, then offers perfect and quasi-perfect conclusions depending on how fully arbitrariness can be removed.

The arbitrariness-inheritance principle is threatened because grounding normally explains what it grounds, and extending inheritance to explanation generally would implausibly make God inherit the arbitrary limits found in creation.
This challenges both the coherence and scope of the new inheritance principle that Rasmussen uses as his principal alternative route to perfection.
Rasmussen's claim that a ground of an arbitrary bounded property inherits that property's arbitrariness and itself calls for explanation.
Schmid distinguishes unexplainedness from comparative arbitrariness, then worries that any sufficiently general inheritance rule would transmit creation's arbitrariness into its divine explanation.

Arbitrariness inheritance should be restricted to strong necessitating grounding and need not apply to indeterministic creative explanations, so a free creator can produce contingent limits without inheriting them.
The distinction is required to preserve the inheritance principle while blocking Schmid's objection that divine creation would make God inherit every arbitrary feature of the world.
Schmid's objection that God would inherit the arbitrariness of creation whenever God grounds or explains creation's contingent limits.
Rasmussen confines the seeping intuition to tight necessitating grounds and contrasts them with creative relations in which reasons and indeterminacy permit one outcome rather than another.

Natural-theological arguments must be held in reflective equilibrium with one's model of God, and grounding divine tripersonality in a deeper divine layer may conflict with traditional divine simplicity.
The argument identifies a significant theological cost of one response to the Trinity objection and constrains which God-models can consistently employ the limits argument.
Rasmussen's suggestion that divine tripersonality may be explained by a deeper ground within fundamental divine reality.
Schmid argues that reasons for theism cannot be divorced from the resulting model of God because positing fundamental and derivative layers within God threatens traditional simplicity.
Reducing arbitrary limits may itself point toward a foundational form of divine simplicity, although its compatibility with other theological models remains an open question.
The suggestion reframes a purported theological cost as a possible constructive implication of the argument while acknowledging unresolved model-specific consequences.
Schmid's concern that deeper grounding layers within God conflict with traditional formulations of divine simplicity.
Rasmussen suggests that the method of removing arbitrary boundaries could support simplicity at the deepest foundation, while leaving its relation to other theological models unsettled.

Removing arbitrary limits from fundamental reality supports a triadic conception of perfection involving maximal power, positivity, and persistence, or at least the greatest degrees of those attributes compatible with eliminating arbitrariness.
This is a direct constructive application of the limits argument to God-like perfection and specifies the principal attributes the argument is claimed to support.
Rasmussen argues that unexplained limits on power, positive value, or continued existence call for further explanation, yielding maximal or minimally arbitrary versions of all three attributes.
A modal variant may require only a possible explanation of limits to reach a possible perfect being, from which modal perfection reasoning could yield an actual perfect being.
The modal route offers an alternative extension of the arbitrary-limits strategy when actual explanations of every limit are unavailable, though Rasmussen notes familiar reservations.
Rasmussen sketches a distinct modal pathway from possible explanations of limits to possible perfection and then to actuality if perfection entails existence across possible worlds.
